summary: Describes the MRT file format for saving routing information, such as routing protocol messages, state changes and the contents of routing tables. It grew out of the Multi-threaded Routing Toolkit and is widely used to archive and analyze BGP data collected from routers.

eli5.summary: Routers keep lots of notes about the best roads for internet traffic. This describes a standard way of writing those notes into a file so scientists can read and study them later.

questions: how to export bgp routing data
what is an mrt record header
how does mrt store bgp updates
subtitle: A standard file format for archiving routing protocol messages and routing table snapshots.

tldr.problem: Researchers and engineers want to study routing protocol traffic and routing table snapshots, but need one standard way to record and archive that data.
tldr.mechanism: Every MRT record starts with a common header (timestamp, type, subtype, length) followed by a message whose layout depends on the type, covering BGP, OSPF and IS-IS messages as well as full BGP routing table dumps.
tldr.outcome: MRT became the archive format behind large BGP data projects such as the University of Oregon Route Views Project and the RIPE NCC Routing Information Service, and the RFC records which older types are deprecated.

today: RFC 6396 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the specification of the MRT format, and RFC 6397 adds an optional geo-location subtype to it.

sections.title: Why MRT Exists
sections.content:
Researchers and engineers often want to analyze network behavior by studying routing protocol transactions and snapshots of the routing information base (RIB). The MRT record format was developed to encapsulate, export and archive this information in one standard representation. The name comes from the Multi-threaded Routing Toolkit, where the format began.

The RFC names two large archival projects built on MRT: the University of Oregon Route Views Project and the RIPE NCC Routing Information Service (RIS). The format was first defined in the MRT Programmer's Guide, and later extensions came from the GNU Zebra software suite and the Sprint Advanced Technology Labs Python Routing Toolkit (PyRT). This RFC writes down the format as it is used.

Multi-octet numbers are encoded in network octet order, most significant octet first. Fields that carry routing message contents appear in the same order as in the original packet.
sections.eli5: Scientists want to study how internet routers talk. MRT is a shared way of saving that conversation in a file, like everyone agreeing to use the same kind of notebook.

sections.title: The MRT Common Header
sections.content:
Every MRT record begins with a Common Header made of four fields: a 4-octet Timestamp, a 2-octet Type, a 2-octet Subtype and a 4-octet Length. A variable-length Message follows. The Length counts the octets of the message and does not include the Common Header itself.

The timestamp is the number of seconds, leap seconds excluded, since midnight proleptic UTC on January 1, 1970 (often called UNIX time). A 4-octet value cannot go past 03:14:07 on January 19, 2038, which is 7FFFFFFF. Implementations that want to write records after that date need an alternate epoch, and the RFC says how to signal one is outside its scope.

Types 0 through 4 are informational messages about the state of an MRT collector. Types 5 and higher carry routing information. The Subtype separates message kinds within one Type.

Some types have a variant with the suffix _ET (Extended Timestamp). These add a 32-bit Microsecond Timestamp right after the Length field. It is an unsigned offset in microseconds added to the Timestamp, and it is counted in the Length value. The Subtype and Message of an _ET type are otherwise the same as the type without the suffix.
sections.eli5: Each saved note starts with a label that says when it was written, what kind of note it is and how long it is. The extended version adds a tiny stopwatch reading for when one second is not precise enough.

sections.title: The Defined MRT Types
sections.content:
The currently defined routing types are OSPFv2 (11), TABLE_DUMP (12), TABLE_DUMP_V2 (13), BGP4MP (16), ISIS (32) and OSPFv3 (48). The types BGP4MP_ET (17), ISIS_ET (33) and OSPFv3_ET (49) are their extended-timestamp variants.

OSPFv2 records encode OSPF packets as defined in RFC 2328. The message holds the remote IP address (the source address of the IP header), the local IP address (the destination address) and then the complete OSPF packet that followed the IP header. OSPFv3 extends this to IPv6 for the protocol in RFC 5340 by adding an Address Family field in front of the two addresses.

ISIS records support IS-IS as defined in RFC 1195. There is no type-specific header and the Subtype is undefined: the IS-IS PDU follows the Common Header directly.
sections.eli5: The file has different kinds of notes: one kind for each routing language the routers speak. Each kind has its own simple form to fill in, and the label on top tells you which form it is.

sections.title: Routing Table Dumps: TABLE_DUMP and TABLE_DUMP_V2
sections.content:
Both table-dump types encode the contents of a BGP Routing Information Base. The older TABLE_DUMP puts each RIB entry in its own record. Its Subtype says whether addresses are IPv4 (1, AFI_IPv4) or IPv6 (2, AFI_IPv6). It has a View Number, a 16-bit Sequence Number that wraps to zero, the prefix and prefix length, a Status octet that SHOULD be 1, an originated time, the peer address, a 2-octet Peer AS, and the BGP attributes. Because of its limits, new encoders are RECOMMENDED to use TABLE_DUMP_V2. Decoders MAY still support the old type because of the volume of historical data.

TABLE_DUMP_V2 adds 4-byte AS number support and full BGP multiprotocol support. It saves space by using an index table of peers and one MRT record per NLRI entry. The dump starts with a PEER_INDEX_TABLE (subtype 1) holding the collector BGP ID, an optional view name (UTF-8) and the list of peers. Each peer's position in that list, starting at 0, is the index used by later records. The RIB records MUST immediately follow it.

Each peer entry has a Peer Type bit field: bit 6 says whether the peer AS number is 16 bits (0) or 32 bits (1), and bit 7 says whether the peer address is IPv4 (0) or IPv6 (1).

The RIB records use subtypes 2 to 5 (RIB_IPV4_UNICAST, RIB_IPV4_MULTICAST, RIB_IPV6_UNICAST, RIB_IPV6_MULTICAST) for the common cases. One record holds a sequence number, the prefix length and prefix, an entry count, and that many RIB entries for the prefix. Subtype 6, RIB_GENERIC, covers anything else with an explicit AFI, SAFI and NLRI. A reader that does not recognize the AFI and SAFI SHOULD discard the rest of the record.

Each RIB entry carries a peer index, an originated time, an attribute length and the BGP attributes. All AS numbers in the AS_PATH MUST be 4-byte. For the MP_REACH_NLRI attribute only the next hop length and next hop address are kept, since the rest is already in the record header.
sections.eli5: A table dump is a photo of a router's whole map of roads. First comes a list of who told the router about each road, with numbers. After that, each road is written down once, using those numbers instead of repeating the names.

sections.title: Recording Live BGP: BGP4MP
sections.content:
The BGP4MP type records live BGP activity. It has six subtypes: BGP4MP_STATE_CHANGE (0), BGP4MP_MESSAGE (1), BGP4MP_MESSAGE_AS4 (4), BGP4MP_STATE_CHANGE_AS4 (5), BGP4MP_MESSAGE_LOCAL (6) and BGP4MP_MESSAGE_AS4_LOCAL (7).

A state change record logs a move in the BGP finite state machine from an Old State to a New State, using the values from RFC 4271: Idle (1), Connect (2), Active (3), OpenSent (4), OpenConfirm (5) and Established (6). It also has the peer and local AS numbers, an optional Interface Index (which MAY be zero) and an Address Family (1 for IPv4, 2 for IPv6) for the two IP addresses.

A message record wraps one complete BGP message, including the 16-octet marker, 2-octet length and 1-octet type, and it can hold any BGP message type. Only one BGP message SHALL be encoded per record. The plain subtypes use 2-byte AS numbers, and the AS_PATH MUST only have 2-byte numbers. The _AS4 subtypes are identical except that the Peer AS and Local AS fields are 4 bytes, and the AS_PATH MUST only have 4-byte numbers.

The _LOCAL subtypes mark messages generated by the collector itself instead of received from a peer. This helps active BGP implementations archive what they sent. The Local fields then describe the collector and the Peer fields describe the recipient.
sections.eli5: This kind of note is like a diary of a router's phone calls with its neighbors. It writes down each message and also when the call went from "dialing" to "connected" or back.

sections.title: Type and Subtype Registries
sections.content:
MRT has two name spaces: Type Codes and Subtype Codes, each 16 bits long. The RFC states that MRT is not a general-purpose export format, and allocations should not be made for purposes unrelated to routing protocol information export.

Type Codes 0 to 64 are reserved, and new codes MUST be allocated starting at 65. Codes 65 to 511 are assigned by IETF Review, 512 to 2047 by Specification Required, and 2048 to 64511 First Come First Served. Codes 64512 to 65534 are for Experimental Use, and 65535 is reserved. Subtype assignments follow the rules of the Type they belong to.

The IANA section also lists the defined subtype codes for each type, including BGP4MP_ENTRY (2) and BGP4MP_SNAPSHOT (3) under BGP4MP, which Appendix B deprecates.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of which label numbers mean what, so two people never use the same number for different things. Some number ranges are kept for experiments.

sections.title: Deprecated Types and Encoding Examples
sections.content:
Appendix B documents types 0 to 10 as deprecated, since some were never known to be implemented or were incompletely specified. They may still interest researchers looking at historical archives. Types 0 to 4 (NULL, START, DIE, I_AM_DEAD, PEER_DOWN) were informational messages meant for sending MRT records to a remote store, and are not known to be implemented. Types 5 to 10 (BGP, RIP, IDRP, RIPNG, BGP4PLUS, BGP4PLUS_01) were superseded. The BGP type and its subtypes are considered deprecated by BGP4MP.

Appendix A is a non-normative set of encoding examples. One shows a BGP4MP_MESSAGE_AS4 record (type 16, subtype 4) with Peer AS 64496 and Local AS 64497, and another shows a RIB_IPV6_UNICAST entry for the prefix 2001:0DB8::/32 with an AS path of 64496 64511 64502.
sections.eli5: Some old kinds of note turned out to be unused, so they are listed as retired. They stay in the book so people can still read very old files.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The MRT fields are descriptive. They are not used to make a receiving application behave in a particular way, so the format itself does not create additional security risks.

The data can still be sensitive. A BGP peer that sends a message to an MRT-enabled router might not expect it to be shared outside the AS it was sent to. Peer IP addresses, BGP next hop addresses and BGP path attributes could help someone mount attacks against BGP, and the RFC points to RFC 4272 for known BGP weaknesses. An organization that publishes MRT dumps beyond its own domain, for example for researchers, should check with the affected peers and possibly remove sensitive fields. The RFC also notes that the geo-location extension in RFC 6397 could reveal where an MRT router's peers are.
sections.eli5: An MRT file is only a record, so it cannot do anything by itself. But it can show who talks to whom, so be careful before sharing it with strangers.
